cards.title: Set Up a Domain Property in Google Search Console
cards.summary: Choose the Domain property type and complete DNS verification so no URL variant of the store slips through tracking.
cards.use_when: Starting organic search measurement for a store, or migrating from an old URL-prefix property that only covers one subdomain or protocol.
steps: Open the property dropdown and add a property, then choose Domain rather than URL prefix. Domain covers every subdomain, www and non-www, plus HTTP and HTTPS, which matters for stores with shop., blog., or checkout subdomains.
Copy the provided TXT record, sign into the registrar (GoDaddy, Namecheap, Cloudflare, etc.) or ask the webmaster, and paste it into DNS settings.
If verification fails immediately, use verify later and retry the next day since DNS changes take time to propagate.
After verification, let data populate, then connect the property to any reporting tools the team already uses so the same click data drives dashboards.
caveats: The Domain option requires DNS access; if a third party controls DNS, expect a short webmaster task.
Search Console only retains 16 months of history, so export older data if you need longer trend lines.

cards.title: Read Overall Search Performance With Compare Mode
cards.summary: Use clicks, impressions, CTR, and average position with a period comparison to answer high-level growth questions on one screen.
cards.use_when: Monthly or quarterly reporting on organic traffic to the store, or when deciding whether a decline needs investigation.
steps: Open Performance > Search results and set the date range; options run from 24 hours to 16 months.
Toggle the metrics you need: total clicks, total impressions, average CTR, average position.
Turn on Compare and set the last three months against the previous period, or six months versus previous when analyzing a specific drop.
Read the chart for growth or decline, the Queries tab for what people type, and the Pages tab for which URLs carry the traffic.
If clicks are up versus the prior period, current activity is working; if down, move to the click-difference sort described in the traffic-drop workflow.
caveats: Average position is averaged across every impression, location and device, so treat it as a trend line, not a fixed rank.
Raw click totals mix branded and non-branded demand, so they overstate what content earned.

cards.title: Isolate Non-Branded Clicks With Custom Regex
cards.summary: Filter out branded queries using a doesn't-match regex so reports show only traffic from people who did not already know the brand.
cards.use_when: Proving content or SEO impact to leadership, or setting traffic goals where branded demand would flatter the numbers.
steps: In Performance, add a query filter and switch the match type to Custom regex.
Choose doesn't match and enter brand terms separated by the pipe symbol, which means OR, e.g. brandname|brand name|brandname com.
Everything branded disappears; what remains is non-branded performance from users who discovered the site through content.
Layer compare mode on top: non-branded clicks last three months versus the previous period, so the chart shows growth or decline in earned traffic.
Use that single number to steer content decisions and monthly reporting rather than raw clicks.
caveats: Branded search still matters on its own, since buyers often discuss purchases with AI assistants and then Google the brand name before buying; track it separately rather than discarding it.
Regex patterns need care with partial matches; review the filtered query list to confirm nothing legitimate was excluded.

cards.title: Diagnose Indexation Status With URL Inspection
cards.summary: Tell apart 'discovered - currently not indexed' and 'crawled - currently not indexed' to decide whether a page needs links, better content, or patience.
cards.use_when: A product, category, or landing page is published but not appearing in Google results.
steps: Paste the page URL into the URL inspection bar; Google reports whether it is indexed, when it was last crawled, and what blocks it.
If the status is Discovered - currently not indexed, Google knows the page exists but has not crawled yet. This is common on new sites; add internal links from stronger pages to speed crawling.
If the status is Crawled - currently not indexed, Google read the page and passed on it, usually a content quality or thinness signal. Strengthen the page before requesting recrawl.
Once fixed, use Request Indexing to prompt a recrawl. There is a daily quota and no guarantee, but it beats waiting.
If the page is not on Google at all, read the stated reason underneath and act on that specific reason rather than guessing.
caveats: On newer or smaller sites, 'crawled - currently not indexed' can reflect overall site authority rather than the page itself; the fix may be patience and authority building, not repeated rewrites.
Request Indexing is quota-limited and not instantaneous.

cards.title: Audit Site-Level Not-Indexed Pages by Reason
cards.summary: Review the Pages report grouped by exclusion reason and confirm each exclusion is deliberate rather than an accident.
cards.use_when: Technical health audits, pre- or post-launch checks, or when organic traffic to key store pages is unexpectedly missing.
steps: Open Indexing > Pages in the sidebar to see every not-indexed URL grouped by reason.
Apply the decision rule: ask whether you want people to find this content on Google. If yes, it should not sit under excluded by noindex tag or blocked by robots.txt.

Confirm that ad landing pages, thank-you and confirmation pages, internal search results, filtered category pages, and staging or test pages are intentionally excluded so paid tracking stays clean and duplicate filters do not compete with primary categories.
Look for surprises: staging pages that slipped through robots.txt before launch, or money pages accidentally noindexed.
Fix only the unintended exclusions; leave deliberate ones alone.
caveats: Not indexed does not equal an error; many exclusions are the system working as intended.
Blocking or noindexing ad landing pages is presented as a recommended practice here because it protects ad tracking, not as a universal rule.

cards.title: Track a Specific Page or Keyword Without a Paid Rank Tracker
cards.summary: Use page and exact-query filters plus compare mode to turn Search Console into a free rank tracker for money pages and target keywords.
cards.use_when: Monitoring ranking movement on a cornerstone product page, category, or a cluster of posts over time.
steps: In Performance, add a filter, choose Page, and paste the exact URL. Turn on average position and the chart becomes that page's ranking history, up to 16 months.
To track one keyword instead, filter by Query and switch to Exact query so one term maps to one line on the chart.
Add compare mode: average position over the last three months versus the previous three months gives a hard delta.
Focus tracking on non-branded queries, since branded terms sit at position one all day and reveal little about competitive standing.
caveats: Average position is averaged across impressions, locations and devices; treat it as a trend, not a pinpoint rank.
Low-volume keywords bounce; a two-position wobble on a keyword with roughly 40 impressions is noise, not a signal.

cards.title: Find the Pages Behind a Traffic Drop
cards.summary: Sort the comparison table by click difference ascending to surface the exact URLs that lost traffic and look for patterns across them.
cards.use_when: Organic traffic fell and the cause is unclear, especially after an algorithm update.
steps: Set the comparison window to cover the drop, e.g. last six months versus the previous period.
Sort the table by click difference ascending so the biggest losers float to the top.
Inspect what the losing pages share: same topic cluster, same page type, thin content, or in the case described, pages cannibalizing each other.
If the pattern is still unclear, consider that the SERP itself changed: users may now demand more depth, a different format, or the query intent itself may have shifted over time.
Fix the identified cause on the affected pages, prioritizing those with the largest click loss.
caveats: The source describes this workflow with a client example, not a guaranteed recovery method.
Search Console alone shows what dropped; deeper competitor and content-gap analysis usually happens in a separate content optimization tool.

cards.title: Re-Target a Page Using Its Own Query Data
cards.summary: Check which queries already generate clicks for a page and align the title and H1 to the query Google is actually rewarding.
cards.use_when: Post-publish optimization of a product page, category, or blog post that targets a keyword in its title tag.
steps: Pick the page, filter Performance by that page's URL, and open the Queries tab to see every query it appears for and which ones produce clicks.

Compare the intended target keyword against the actual click leaders. In the example, 'beeswax good for your skin' produced about three clicks in three months while 'benefits of beeswax for skin' produced 19, which signals the keyword the page should target.
Rewrite the title and H1 around the query with demonstrated click demand.
Then examine the pages currently ranking for that keyword to see what yours lacks: terms covered, headings, questions answered, and depth.
Re-crawl the updated page via URL inspection after the changes go live.
caveats: The click figures are a single case example, so expect different magnitudes on your own data.
Manual rewriting can be slow and does not account for AI visibility; the source recommends a content optimization tool for the gap analysis part.

cards.title: Mine Question Queries for FAQ and Content Ideas
cards.summary: Regex-filter question-word queries to find real questions the site already surfaces for, then build direct answers.
cards.use_when: Planning FAQ sections, support content, or new pages that should answer buyer questions explicitly.
steps: In Performance, add a query filter and switch to Custom regex.
Match question words such as who, what, when, where, why, how, can, does.
Review the returned queries and for each ask whether any page of yours answers it directly.
Where the answer is no, the site currently ranks only on a passing mention. Add an FAQ section to the relevant page, or write a dedicated page if the topic warrants it.
Prefer structured, direct answers over mentions buried in prose, since this format is also what AI features tend to draw on.
caveats: Ranking on a passing mention still means the site appears for the query; the gain comes from answering directly, not from the query being unknown.
Question words vary by language and phrasing, so adjust the pattern beyond the listed English terms.

cards.title: Get Backlink and Internal Link Data Free From Search Console
cards.summary: Use the Links report for most-linked pages, internal link counts, and referring sites, then route authority toward pages you want to rank.
cards.use_when: Planning internal linking during a product launch or category push, or auditing which pages carry authority.
steps: Click Links in the sidebar to see most-linked pages, internal link counts, and which sites link to you, at no cost.
Click into any page to see the exact sites linking to it.
Identify high-authority pages, since internal links distribute backlink equity across the site.
Point internal links from those authority pages at newer or more strategic pages you are trying to rank, such as launch pages or priority categories.
caveats: The Links report is shallower than dedicated backlink tools: no competitor data and no link quality scores.
The source accepts that brand mentions matter but argues links remain an important ranking signal; it does not treat mentions as a full replacement.

cards.title: Fix Video Indexing by Building Dedicated Watch Pages
cards.summary: Give important videos their own page where the video is the main event so Google indexes the video, not just the page.
cards.use_when: Publishing product demos, tutorials, or reviews that should earn video results and thumbnails.
steps: Open the Videos report under Indexing to see which indexed pages contain videos Google indexed, and the stated reason for the ones it did not.
When the reason is 'video isn't on a watch page', apply the underlying rule: Google indexes a video when the video is the main event of the page.
Model the layout on a YouTube watch page: video front and center above the fold, with watching it the whole reason for visiting.
Move best-performing videos off mid-post embeds, sidebars, or tiny players onto dedicated pages for those videos.
Leave blog-post embeds in place if they serve readers, but accept they yield a normal page result rather than video results.
caveats: A page with an embedded video can still rank normally; what is lost is the video result, video thumbnail, and video search tab placement.
The watch-page rule is the source's stated reason Google most commonly gives, not a guarantee that every dedicated page gets indexed.

cards.title: Use the Discover and Google News Reports for Non-Query Traffic
cards.summary: Read feeds-driven traffic separately, because Discover and News show pages and impressions rather than queries.
cards.use_when: Checking whether visual, timely, or list-driven store content earns traffic outside classic search.
steps: Open the Discover report to see whether Google featured your content in the phone feed; there are no queries because Discover pushes content based on interests, so you get pages and impressions instead.
Open the Google News report, which works the same way, and check whether its numbers are significant for your content type.
If your content skews timely, visual, or list-driven, treat Discover as a channel that can outdraw search traffic and is only visible in this report.
Use the page-level data to decide which content formats to repeat.
caveats: Discover and News traffic is not query-driven, so you cannot mine keywords from these reports.
The source notes the numbers can be significant for certain content types but provides no benchmark.

cards.title: Diagnose Falling Clicks With Stable Rankings
cards.summary: When positions hold but clicks shrink, check CTR against position to decide between a snippet refresh and an AI-overview answer stealing the click.
cards.use_when: Organic clicks decline while rank tracking shows no meaningful position loss.
steps: Compare CTR against position for the affected pages over time.

If a page holds position three but CTR has been shrinking for months, one of two things is happening: your title and meta description have gone stale while competitors improved theirs, which is an easy snippet rewrite; or something now sits above you answering the question before anyone scrolls, most likely an AI overview.
Open the generative AI performance report and check the pages losing clicks: if they register heavy AI impressions, the content is being read inside Google's AI answers rather than on your site.
If it is a snippet problem, rewrite the title and meta description; if it is an AI answer, treat the content as an AI magnet and consider producing more structured, direct answers on buyer topics.
Consider that losing the click may not mean losing the sale, since the source frames AI visibility as still winning attention even without a site visit.
caveats: The generative AI report is in beta, may not yet be available on your property, and initially shows impressions only, with click and position data promised later.
The report covers only Google's own AI ecosystem and does not show what the AI actually said or whether you were recommended versus name-dropped alongside competitors.

cards.title: Read the Generative AI Performance Report for AEO Benchmarks
cards.summary: Use Google's AI visibility report to see impressions inside AI Overviews and AI mode, broken down by page, country, and device.
cards.use_when: Assessing how much of your content is being consumed in AI answers, or deciding whether to opt out of AI features.
steps: Open the generative AI performance report, shipped in beta, and check whether it is rolled out to your property yet.
Read impressions: how many times a link to your site appeared inside a generative AI feature, broken down by page, country, and device.
Sort by impressions and study the top pages to learn what the AI already favors. Direct, clearly structured answers are the pattern described as AI magnets.
Apply the same structure and directness to the topics buyers ask about, since being the source the AI quotes beats being invisible in it.

If considering Google's toggle to pull content out of AI Overviews and AI mode without affecting normal rankings, use this report as the data for that decision, since it shows exactly how much AI visibility you would give up page by page.
caveats: The report is beta, shows impressions only, and covers only Google's AI surfaces; it says nothing about ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, or Claude.
The opt-out toggle began with UK site owners and was rolling out globally; verify availability before relying on it.
The source does not recommend opting out of AI features.

cards.title: Build a Content Plan From Exported Query Data
cards.summary: Export queries, compare them against your sitemap, and ask an LLM where coverage gaps exist.
cards.use_when: The content calendar is empty and you need new product-page, category, or blog topics grounded in real search demand.
steps: In Performance, export all queries to a spreadsheet; the interface allows up to 1,000 rows.
Provide that list to an AI assistant together with your sitemap.xml file.
Ask where the gaps are: searches where the site surfaces but no page properly covers the topic.
The result is a list of queries already generating visibility for which you have no dedicated coverage, which are lower-risk topics than entirely new keyword research.
Turn each gap into either an FAQ section on an existing page or a new page, depending on how much the topic deserves.
caveats: The export is capped at 1,000 rows, so large sites see a partial query list.
The LLM output is a starting list; validate demand and difficulty before committing production time.

cards.title: Track Rankings Automatically and Flag Refresh Candidates
cards.summary: Set up monitoring that flags pages slipping to positions 6-8 and pages whose rankings drop over a 7-day stretch.
cards.use_when: Managing a large content library where manually filtering Search Console for every page is impractical.
steps: Connect Search Console to a tracking or content optimization tool so it consumes the same performance data.
Configure alerting for pages that have slipped back to pages 6 through 8 of the search results, described as the band a content refresh can usually recover.
Configure alerts for a page whose ranking drops over a 7-day stretch.
Set a quarterly traffic goal in the connected dashboard and track progress plus the daily clicks needed to hit it.
Keep an activity log of what you changed and when Google updates hit, so movement on the chart can be attributed to your work.
caveats: The pages 6-8 band and the 7-day drop window are the source's described tooling heuristics, not universal thresholds; verify the current settings in whichever tool you use.
Tool features and interfaces change; confirm current behavior before configuring alerts.

cards.title: Split Branded From Non-Branded in Ongoing Reporting
cards.summary: Keep branded search visible as its own metric while excluding it from earned-traffic reporting.
cards.use_when: Building a recurring organic dashboard or content KPI set for a store.
steps: Report non-branded clicks with compare mode as the earned-content metric, since branded clicks come from people who already knew the brand and would have arrived anyway.

Track branded search separately as its own KPI. The source argues this matters more in AI-first search, because buyers often hold purchase discussions with AI assistants in separate ecosystems and then Google the brand name when ready to buy.
In a connected dashboard, use a single filter to split branded from non-branded rather than maintaining two manual reports.
Review both lines together: branded volume can indicate AI-driven demand building even when non-branded content metrics look flat.
caveats: The source explicitly separates this from non-branded reporting and says branded keywords sitting at position one reveal almost nothing about ranking position.
The claim that branded search is more important than ever in AI search is the presenter's interpretation, not a measured benchmark.

cards.title: Add Social Accounts as Search Console Properties
cards.summary: Use platform properties to see which search terms lead people to social posts, even for an account with no website attached.
cards.use_when: Attributing search-driven discovery to Instagram, TikTok, X, or YouTube content that feeds the store funnel.
steps: Add your social accounts as their own properties in Search Console, using the platform properties feature announced by Google.
Once enabled, view which search terms lead people to your posts and how those posts perform in Google Search and Discover.
Pair this with a social analytics platform to close the loop: Search Console shows how social content performs on Google, while the social tool shows performance everywhere else.
Use the query terms driving social post discovery to inform both social content and site content topics.
caveats: The source states this was rolling out gradually and none of the presenter's properties had access at the time; check back if it is missing.
This is a new feature whose interface may change; verify current availability in your account.

cards.title: Map AI Visibility Beyond Google With a Brand Tracker
cards.summary: Supplement Google's AI report by tracking brand mentions and citations across major AI models.
cards.use_when: AEO reporting where you need to know whether you are recommended, how you are described, and which sources models cite.
steps: Use a dedicated AI brand tracker to monitor your brand across major AI models, since Search Console covers only Google's AI surfaces.
Track how often you are mentioned and in what sentiment, which competitors beat you, and which sources the models trust most.

For the prompts you track, identify which of your pages the AI actually cites. A citation means the model used your page to build its answer, which is a stronger signal than an AI crawler hitting your server logs.
Compare citation patterns against your structured-answer content to decide what to produce next.
caveats: Search Console's AI report cannot tell you what the AI said, only that your link appeared; recommendation versus name-drop is invisible there.
Server log hits from AI bots are weaker evidence than citations, because a crawl does not mean the model used the page.
